article.title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
article.subtitle: They’re polling surprisingly strongly in some Senate races. But should you bet on those numbers falling back to earth? Plus, some quick thoughts on…

extraction.summary: Model Talk responding to Patrick Ruffini's finding that summer Senate polls from 2018 to 2024 overrated Democrats by about 5 points in late August. Silver gives 13 counterpoints and explains FLIPR's defenses. The data is effectively n=4 cycles. FLIPR assumes correlated but symmetric polling error. Classic and Deluxe assume summer polls revert toward fundamentals. The priors and the likely-voter adjustment already account for turnout. National drift is smaller under polarization. Summer 'silly season' internal polls are penalized. Selection bias affects which races get polled, so the generic ballot is the model's backbone. The post also explains how FLIPR handles Alaska's top-four primary results and ranked-choice transfers, and how Florida's primary moved Democratic odds from 21 to 11 percent.

findings.statement: FLIPR assumes correlated polling errors are fairly common, so one party may sweep most toss-ups as Trump did the 2024 swing states. It also assumes these systematic errors are unpredictable and symmetric, equally likely to favor either party over the long run. Silver calls this a big but deliberate assumption.
findings.evidence_quote: It also assumes, however, that these errors are equally likely to benefit Republicans or Democrats.

findings.statement: Classic and Deluxe treat August polls as not being an unbiased estimator of the November result: they take a weighted average of polls and fundamentals, so a race at R+3 in polls and D+7 in fundamentals might be projected around D+1. The forecast is not a 'now-cast'; reversion toward partisan fundamentals is expected.
findings.rationale: August reflects a different information environment, with fewer ads and partisan cues.
findings.evidence_quote: Classic and Deluxe FLIPR assume that summer polling can be predictably biased.

findings.statement: In mid-August 2026 FLIPR's national environment was about D+7.5, and its historical regression prior predicted about D+8.5, consistent with a midterm against a president at 38 percent approval and with lame-duck presidents' history.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR thinks the current national environment is around D +7.5

findings.statement: Poll-error datasets spanning many polls but few cycles are effectively small samples, because errors are heavily correlated within a cycle; Ruffini's summer-bias data is closer to n=4 than n=hundreds.
findings.evidence_quote: So in some ways, this is closer to n=4 than n=hundreds.

findings.statement: Polls considerably overestimated Democrats in 2020 and 2024 but were accurate and unbiased by historical standards in the 2018 and 2022 midterms. The generic ballot has historically overstated Democrats early in cycles but also understated the opposition party, so long-term trends conflict.
findings.evidence_quote: the polls were both quite accurate and quite unbiased by historical standards in the past two midterms, 2018 and 2022.

findings.statement: One 2026 change to FLIPR was assuming more muted shifts in the national environment when partisanship is high, since late swings in historical generic ballot data have become less frequent: voters lock in earlier and there are fewer true swing voters.
findings.rationale: Partisanship combined with the 24/7 news cycle.
findings.evidence_quote: one of the changes we made to FLIPR this year was to assume more muted shifts in the national environment when partisanship is high

findings.statement: Summer is 'silly season' for polls: campaigns release internal polls for attention and fundraising, and by fall pollsters publish fewer outliers and herd more. FLIPR's harsh penalties on internal polls smooth its averages.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR applies some pretty harsh penalties to internal polls

findings.statement: Race polls suffer selection bias: surprising races such as South Carolina in 2020 get heavily polled, while lopsided ones are ignored. The average Senate race is slightly red because small states have equal representation. The generic ballot is therefore a more common denominator, and FLIPR treats it as the reliable backbone of the national estimate.
findings.evidence_quote: This is why the generic ballot is such a useful instrument, and why FLIPR and other models treat it as a reliable backbone

findings.statement: If one party front-loads advertising in summer, polls could show a temporary 'sugar high'. In principle a model could adjust polls for the partisan ad share during fieldwork, but FLIPR does not, since reliable ad data is hard to get. Silver thinks paid advertising's impact is overrated and hits diminishing returns quickly.
findings.evidence_quote: In the perfect world, FLIPR might even adjust its polling averages based on the partisan share of advertising running while the poll was in the field.

findings.statement: After Alaska's top-four primary, FLIPR uses primary results mainly to forecast vote shares within each party for November. It derives only limited information on aggregate party shares, by comparing parties' relative primary performance across the House, Senate and governor races; aggregate party shares come from general-election polls plus priors. The post-primary logic mirrors FLIPR's code for California and Washington top-two primaries, adjusted for four-way incentives.
findings.evidence_quote: The model uses primary results in Alaska in a slightly complicated way, but it’s mostly to forecast November vote shares within the same party.

findings.statement: In ranked-choice voting, eliminated candidates' votes do not all flow to same-party candidates: a fair number are exhausted because voters rank too few names, and some go to other parties. FLIPR models this, and judged a tie between two Democrats slightly worse for Democrats than one clear leader.
findings.evidence_quote: A fair number of these votes are wasted because voters don’t list enough names on the ballot, and some will go to candidates from other parties instead.

findings.statement: When Angie Nixon (under $1 million raised, DSA member) beat Alexander Vindman (over $16 million raised) in Florida's Democratic Senate primary, FLIPR Deluxe's Democratic odds fell from 21 to 11 percent, partly via expert rating changes. Silver suspects FLIPR may have over-credited Vindman's fundraising even though it discounts out-of-state money. FLIPR makes no special provision for similar candidate names on ballots.

quantities.name: FL D win prob with Vindman
FL D win prob with Nixon

findings.evidence_quote: Democrats’ chances in Florida have fallen from 21 percent with Vindman to 11 percent with Nixon

findings.statement: Much of the historical Democratic bias in midterm summer polls reflected lower Democratic turnout captured only when pollsters switched to likely-voter screens. FLIPR and its predecessors always applied an LV adjustment for this. The Republican turnout advantage may now have flipped because Democrats' college-educated coalition votes reliably in midterms.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR and its various predecessors have therefore always made a likely-voter adjustment

findings.statement: Historical summer polling leads that faded: Phil Bredesen led Marsha Blackburn in Tennessee in August 2018 before losing by 11, and Jaime Harrison tied Lindsey Graham into September 2020 before losing by 10. In 2022, race-level polls were too optimistic for Democrats in summer but converged toward the generic ballot by November.
findings.evidence_quote: The individual-race polls converged toward the generic ballot

political_insights.insight: The traditional Republican midterm turnout edge may have flipped to Democrats, because college graduates, now central to the Democratic coalition, vote at high rates in midterms.
political_insights.evidence: In 2026 most paired LV/RV polls showed Democrats gaining in the LV version.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Reconsider the sign of likely-voter adjustment priors.

political_insights.topic: Florida no longer a swing state
political_insights.insight: Democrats largely wrote off Florida in 2026; FLIPR judged even Kansas a better reach state.

references.description: Patrick Ruffini newsletter on summer Senate polls overrating Democrats (2018-2024)

open_questions: Exact weighting between polls and fundamentals as a function of days to the election.
Size of FLIPR's internal-poll penalty beyond the 4-point historical bias prior.
